content: To prevent work-related mental health conditions, it is essential to implement psychosocial risk management strategies. These include organizational interventions aimed at reshaping working conditions, workplace culture, and interpersonal relationships within the work environment. Promoting and protecting mental health at work requires targeted training and interventions. These should focus on improving mental health literacy, equipping workers with the skills to recognize and address mental health conditions in the workplace, and empowering employees to seek appropriate support when needed. Supporting workers with mental health conditions involves ensuring their full and equitable participation in the workforce. This can be achieved through reasonable accommodations, return-to-work programs, and supported employment initiatives that facilitate their reintegration and sustained engagement in work. Creating an enabling environment for mental health at work necessitates cross-cutting actions. These include leadership commitment, adequate investment, upholding workers' rights, integrating mental health into workplace policies, fostering participation, utilizing evidence-based approaches, and ensuring compliance with established standards. As of 2022, nearly 60% of the global population is engaged in work. All workers have the fundamental right to a safe and healthy working environment. While work can serve as a protective factor for mental health, it can also contribute to harm if not managed appropriately. Mental health conditions, whether work-related or not, have far-reaching impacts on workers, their families, enterprises, and entire economies. The relationship between mental health and work is deeply interconnected. A safe and healthy workplace supports mental well-being, while good mental health enables individuals to work productively. Conversely, unsafe or unhealthy work environments can undermine mental health, and poor mental health can impair a person's ability to work effectively if left unsupported. Globally, 15% of working-age adults live with a mental disorder. Mental health conditions manifest differently across individuals, with varying levels of difficulty and distress. Without effective support systems, these conditions can negatively impact self-confidence, job satisfaction, work capacity, attendance, and employability. Caregivers and family members are also affected by the ripple effects of unsupported mental health conditions. Despite its importance, mental health in the workplace is often misunderstood, underfunded, and deprioritized compared to physical health. Stigma and discrimination against individuals with mental health conditions remain widespread, creating barriers to employment and support. Many employers hesitate to hire individuals with mental health conditions, and workers may avoid disclosing their struggles due to fear of negative career consequences. Workplace losses and missed opportunities due to mental health issues affect individual and household income, while also imposing broader societal costs. These include increased unemployment, reduced productivity, loss of skilled labor, and diminished tax revenue. Addressing mental health at work is therefore critical for both individual well-being and economic stability. Workplaces can either enhance or undermine mental health. Decent work provides income, structured routines, positive relationships, and a sense of purpose and achievement. For individuals with severe mental health conditions, employment can promote recovery, improve self-esteem, and enhance social functioning. Safe and healthy work environments are not only a fundamental right but also contribute to better performance, productivity, staff retention, and reduced workplace conflict. On the other hand, unemployment, job insecurity, workplace discrimination, and poor working conditions are significant sources of stress and risk to mental health. These factors are associated with increased rates of suicide attempts and exacerbate existing mental health conditions. Inequalities in earnings, opportunities, and respect at work further compound these risks, particularly for marginalized groups. Psychosocial risks in the workplace, such as unclear roles, low decision-making authority, and exposure to violence or harassment, can lead to burnout, anxiety, depression, and even suicidal behaviors. Limited access to essential workplace services, such as clean drinking water and safe environments, further undermines mental and physical health. Workers in low-paid, insecure, or isolated jobs, as well as those in the informal economy, face heightened exposure to psychosocial risks. These risks are exacerbated by a lack of structural support, unsafe working conditions, long hours, and limited access to social protections. Informal workers are particularly vulnerable, as they often operate without regulatory safeguards for health and safety. Recent transformations in the world of work, including technological advancements, globalization, and demographic shifts, have introduced new psychosocial risks or intensified existing ones. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated these changes, disrupting labor markets, increasing financial instability, and prompting widespread restructuring of enterprises. For many workers, these changes have resulted in job losses and heightened mental health challenges. Addressing mental health at work requires a comprehensive approach that includes prevention, protection, and support. Preventing work-related mental health conditions involves reshaping work environments to minimize psychosocial risks. Protecting and promoting mental health requires raising awareness, building skills, and fostering early intervention. Supporting workers with mental health conditions involves providing accommodations, return-to-work programs, and supported employment initiatives. Governments, employers, and workers all have roles to play in creating safe and healthy workplaces. This includes implementing evidence-based interventions, tackling stigma and discrimination, and ensuring compliance with occupational safety and health (OSH) standards. International frameworks, such as the ILO Conventions on OSH, provide guidance on protecting both physical and mental health in the workplace. At the national level, governments can establish and enforce laws and policies that promote mental health at work. This includes regulations on OSH, equality, non-discrimination, and workplace violence. Strengthening labor inspection capacities and ensuring compliance with these regulations are essential for safeguarding workers' mental health. Despite these efforts, only 35% of countries currently report having a national program for work-related mental health promotion and prevention. All stakeholders in the world of work must do more to address poor mental health in the workplace. Collaborative actions between governments, employers, and workers' organizations are necessary to drive meaningful improvements in mental health at work.
